trustBoundary: Original instructional content aligned to the five extracted Cambridge 9708 AS 1.3 outcomes. It is not official Cambridge material or an independently verified complete syllabus lesson. Teacher review required before publication.
learningObjectives: Define land, labour, capital and enterprise.
Distinguish human capital from physical capital.
Identify the rewards to each factor of production.
Explain division of labour and specialisation.
Explain the entrepreneur's role in risk-taking and organising other factors.

lesson.prompt: A maize farm uses a field, farm workers, a tractor and a business owner who organises production. Identify the four different productive resources.

lesson.heading: 1. Factors of production
lesson.body: Factors of production are the resources used to produce goods and services. The four categories are land, labour, capital and enterprise. They are not four types of finished product. They describe inputs that are combined in production. A firm needs suitable resources, and those resources have alternative uses. The quantity and quality of available factors influence what an economy can produce. In practice, production usually requires several factors working together rather than one factor acting alone.

lesson.heading: 2. Land
lesson.body: In economics, land means natural resources used in production, not only the physical ground beneath a building. It includes soil, forests, water, minerals, sunlight and other gifts of nature. A farmer uses fertile soil and water; a mining company uses mineral deposits; a tourism business may use natural landscapes. Land is limited and differs in quality and location. Its economic reward is rent.

lesson.heading: 3. Labour
lesson.body: Labour is the human effort, physical or mental, used to produce goods and services. It includes the work of a builder, teacher, nurse, engineer, farm worker or software developer. The quantity of labour depends partly on the size of the workforce, while its quality depends on factors such as education, training, experience, health and motivation. The economic reward to labour is wages or salaries.

lesson.heading: 4. Capital
lesson.body: Capital, as a factor of production, means man-made resources used to produce other goods and services. Examples include machinery, tools, factory buildings, delivery vehicles and computers used by a business. Money used to buy equipment is finance for acquiring capital; money itself is not the physical capital good. The economic reward to capital is interest.

lesson.heading: 5. Physical capital and human capital
lesson.body: Physical capital consists of produced assets used in production, such as a tractor, computer or factory machine. Human capital is the knowledge, skills, abilities and experience embodied in people that make their labour more productive. A trained electrician represents human capital; the testing equipment used by that electrician is physical capital. Education and training can increase human capital. Do not confuse human capital with the number of workers.

lesson.heading: 6. Enterprise
lesson.body: Enterprise is the factor that brings the other factors of production together and makes decisions about how they will be used. The entrepreneur identifies an opportunity, organises resources, makes decisions and bears the risk that the business may not earn enough revenue to cover its costs. For example, a person may combine land, workers, machinery and finance to establish a food-processing business. The economic reward to enterprise is profit, although the entrepreneur may also make a loss.

lesson.heading: Worked example: a small food-processing business
lesson.scenario: A business processes locally grown groundnuts into packaged peanut butter.
reasoning: Land: the groundnuts, water and site used in production are natural resources.
Labour: workers operate equipment, package products and manage sales.
Capital: processing machinery, storage equipment and delivery vehicles are physical capital.
Enterprise: the owner organises the inputs, makes decisions and accepts the risk of uncertain sales.
Rewards: rent for land, wages for labour, interest for capital and profit for enterprise.
lesson.caution: A person can perform more than one role. Classify the resource or function being described, not simply the person's job title.

lesson.heading: 7. Division of labour
lesson.body: Division of labour occurs when a production process is split into separate tasks and different workers specialise in particular tasks. In a food-processing line, one worker may prepare ingredients, another operate the machine, another package products and another check quality. Each worker becomes more practised at a narrower task. This can increase output per worker, save time switching between tasks and make it easier to train workers for specific roles.

lesson.heading: 8. Specialisation
lesson.body: Specialisation means concentrating on a particular task, skill, product or economic activity. Division of labour is one way specialisation occurs within a production process. Specialised workers may become faster and more accurate through repetition and practice. Specialisation can also occur between firms, regions and countries when they focus on goods or services they can produce relatively effectively. Production then relies on exchange and cooperation between specialised producers.

lesson.heading: Worked example: a school uniform workshop
lesson.scenario: A workshop changes from each worker making a complete uniform to a production line with separate cutting, stitching, buttoning and quality-checking tasks.
reasoning: Tasks are divided into distinct stages.
Workers specialise and gain practice in their stage.
Less time may be lost switching between unrelated tasks.
The workshop may produce more uniforms per day if stages are coordinated effectively.
lesson.caution: Specialisation does not guarantee higher output in every situation. A machine breakdown or delay at one stage can interrupt the whole production line.

lesson.heading: 9. Keep the four factors distinct
lesson.body: Land is natural resources; labour is human effort; capital is man-made equipment used to produce; enterprise organises the process and bears business risk. A tractor is capital, the operator's work is labour, the farmer who coordinates the business performs enterprise, and the field is land. The same production activity can contain all four factors at once.

lesson.heading: 10. Combine the factors
lesson.body: Production depends on combining factors in a suitable way. More machinery may raise the amount of capital per worker; training may improve human capital; better organisation may improve how inputs are used. Division of labour and specialisation can raise productivity by allowing workers to focus on tasks. The entrepreneur decides how to organise these inputs while facing uncertainty. The four factor rewards describe the incomes received by the owners of the respective factors.

retrievalCheck.prompt: Which factor of production includes water, forests and mineral deposits?
What is the difference between physical capital and human capital?
Match land, labour, capital and enterprise to their usual economic rewards.
How does division of labour create specialisation?
What distinguishes the entrepreneur's role from the other factors?

practice.prompt: Define the four factors of production.
answer: capital man-made resources used in production
enterprise organising factors and bearing risk
practice.misconception: Capital is not simply money, and land includes more than physical ground.

practice.prompt: Distinguish human capital from physical capital, using one example of each.
answer: human capital knowledge skills experience embodied in people
practice.misconception: A trained worker is human capital; the machine they use is physical capital.

practice.prompt: A firm rents a factory site, employs machine operators, borrows to buy equipment and is organised by an owner who accepts the risk of uncertain sales. Identify the factor of production and reward in each case.
marking: 1 mark for each correct factor and reward pairing
practice.misconception: Do not assign the factory site to capital when the question refers to the natural resource/land input; factory buildings and equipment are capital.

practice.prompt: Explain how division of labour may increase productivity in a clothing workshop.
answer: less time switching tasks or greater efficiency
marking: up to 2 marks explain productivity mechanism
practice.misconception: Do not simply state that workers work harder. Explain how task specialisation can raise output per worker.

practice.prompt: Explain why the entrepreneur is a distinct factor of production.
practice.misconception: Enterprise is not merely owning equipment; it involves organising resources and accepting business risk.

requiredEvidence: explain the productivity mechanism of division of labour
explain the entrepreneur's organising and risk-bearing role

visuals.title: The four factors of production and their rewards
visuals.purpose: Connect each factor's meaning to its usual economic reward.
visuals.altText: Land is natural resources and earns rent; labour is human effort and earns wages; capital is man-made productive assets and earns interest; enterprise organises resources and bears risk, earning profit.

visuals.title: Division of labour and specialisation
visuals.purpose: Visualise a production process divided into specialised stages.
visuals.altText: A production process is split into separate tasks, workers specialise in individual stages, repetition builds skill and speed, and coordinated output may increase.
